papers.title: Questions, Explanation and Synthesis in Service Mathematics: Course Design with Didactic Units and Hybrid Teaching
papers.abstract: Students may have access to a convincing mathematical explanation without being able to reconstruct or adapt it. A course must provide opportunities to develop that understanding while keeping the work sustainable for students and teachers. This article develops a methodology for service mathematics in which a question ledger guides both course authoring and classroom decisions. Course-relative didactic units organise explanatory purposes, prerequisites and connections, initially calibrated by a five-to-seven-minute expert account. Teaching combines preparation, student exposition and supported repair with substantial teacher exposition and synthesis. Their allocation changes with the topic, audience and conditions of teaching. Compression and recovery explain how developed constructions become reusable while their grounds remain accessible. Three analyses from mathematics for computing-full Sudoku encoding, grayscale projection and a software failure contract-show how contrasting cases guide explanation and revision. The practice-informed contribution connects coherent course design with adaptable teaching and manageable preparation, and identifies questions for evaluating learning, participation and sustained teacher effort.

papers.title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step
papers.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.

papers.title: Investigating Shadow IT Use and Adoption in Educational Institutions and their Privacy Implications
papers.abstract: Digital technologies have become ubiquitous in education, integrated to nearly all aspects of teaching, learning, research, and communication. They collect enormous amounts of data from their users, primarily students. When procured institutionally, data collection and use are guided by legally binding contracts. However, recent studies suggest that apps found on the open web are increasingly being used for teaching and evaluation without going through a formal audit, raising concerns about privacy, security, and regulatory compliance. How prevalent such shadow IT use in education is, and what privacy and compliance risks they create remain unexplored. We address this gap through a sequential survey-based study: one survey with 375 educators and another with 21 system administrators at K-12 or HEIs (Higher Education Institutes). We discover widespread use of external apps by educators: 1,373 apps were reported, 494 among them were unique, primarily used for pedagogical utility (n=213) and functional convenience (n=155). Their adoption and integration are often facilitated, even encouraged, by administrators; this result deviates from studies in other domains (e.g., industry) where admins actively prevent them. Many educators (n=62) continued using apps they do not trust, citing a lack of alternatives or dependency as barriers to discontinuation. We also found that fewer than one in three educators were aware of institutional policies on shadow IT use (K-12: 30.3%, HEI: 24.8%), and 22 knowingly violated such policies. While 107 received formal warnings for using shadow IT, only 33 adjusted their behavior. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings and future recommendations for various stakeholders to minimize the risks.

papers.title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents
papers.abstract: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to 13.7% and required state-check failures from 63 to 1 across 180 trials. The resulting policy outperforms seven reference baselines by over 20 points while reducing output tokens by 17-39% across seven of eight external benchmarks without regressing on general reasoning or tool use.

papers.title: Faculty Experience with Generative AI Integration into the Teaching and Learning Process
papers.abstract: This study was conducted to enhance our knowledge and understanding of the lived experiences of faculty regarding generative artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and learning within the English and Communication Program at the American University of Armenia. This phenomenological qualitative research study used face-to-face, in-depth, open-ended interviews with five faculty members from the program. Faculty expressed different levels of conflict, voicing both positive and negative issues and concerns regarding their experiences with generative AI in the teaching and learning process. Five categories and 11 themes emerged from the analysis of these interviews, including concerns about academic integrity and student learning, as well as a lack of faculty AI training, understanding, and experience. Emergent themes indicated that faculty need additional support, including training and leadership guidance, in order to better understand the importance and benefits of effective AI utilization and AI literacy development. Faculty lacked sufficient experience with and understanding of generative AI capabilities and ongoing developments. Overall, faculty perceptions and attitudes toward generative AI within teaching and learning can be characterized as a mix of reservation and optimism.

papers.title: Feedback-Driven Prompt Refinement for Educational AI: Affective Trajectory Estimation and Bloom's Taxonomy Classification
papers.abstract: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.

papers.title: Shaderous: A Browser-based Hydrodynamics Code for Physics Research and Teaching
papers.abstract: Shaderous is a three-dimensional code for compressible gas dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics that runs in WebGPU compute shaders in a web browser on any vendor's GPU. It combines an unsplit MUSCL-Hancock scheme and HLLC fluxes with a multigrid Poisson solver, block-structured adaptive mesh refinement with per-block timesteps, constrained transport with HLLD fluxes, point masses with sinks, gray radiation transport with the M1 closure, implicit pressure for low Mach numbers, tabulated equations of state from degenerate electrons to rock and iron, cooling, viscosity, conduction, resistivity, mixtures of gases, and nuclear burning by a neural network trained on a 13-isotope reaction network. A setup is shared as a link and runs on a student's own laptop or phone, so the code suits teaching at every level. A run is limited to one GPU: the largest adaptive mesh so far held about 175 million cells on an NVIDIA H200. It therefore suits parameter studies, run as sweeps from the command line, rather than the largest single simulations. Three aspects of the design are, as far as we can find, new. First, the hydrodynamic solver stores no face flux. The two cells that share a face compute bit-identical fluxes, so cells at boundaries between levels and between timesteps recompute their neighbors' fluxes instead of keeping a flux register. Mass, momentum and energy are conserved to round-off on the adaptive mesh, and compensated sums keep the divergence of the magnetic field at round-off. Second, the whole step runs on the GPU: the timestep and the assignment of blocks to time bins are reduced there, and ghost cells are computed as they are loaded rather than exchanged. Third, the code computes in single precision yet reproduces a range of astrophysical systems accurately, from stars and atmospheres in hydrostatic balance to shocks, gravitational collapse and magnetized flows, in 206 validation tests.

papers.title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
papers.abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

papers.title: Reducing Authorship Attribution Risk in Student Texts Through Style-Conditioned Rewriting
papers.abstract: Building NLP applications for education is constrained by data scarcity due to student privacy concerns and data regulations. To address this, we propose a style-aware approach to rewriting student forum posts that retains analytical value while reducing identifiability. Our method isolates content, structure, and style as separate conditioning channels and aggregates over student-disjoint exemplar partitions within style clusters, extending Differentially Private In-context Learning (DP-ICL) with cluster-restricted retrieval. Across three educational NLP datasets, our approach achieves high style fidelity, preserves downstream task performance, and reduces authorship attribution risk relative to the original student-written texts, including against a dedicated authorship-attribution model.

papers.title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
papers.abstract: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

papers.title: One machine, three drawings: a didactic analysis of a teaching progression for the function concept from Grade 4 to Grade 10
papers.abstract: The function concept can be entered through a correspondence between sets, a relation that is single-valued, or through a process that turns an input into an output. This paper presents the design rationale and a critical analysis of a source progression for functions (Grades 4-10, nominal ages 9-16, with two levels on relations between quantities), from which French-curriculum and International Baccalaureate chapters published at https://commeunjeu.org are assembled. One schema is presented first and kept throughout: a function is a machine that takes an input, applies a rule and gives exactly one output. Its drawing changes with age (a robot, then a box, then the arrow $f : x \mapsto f(x)$), and each change is shown once, the two drawings side by side; after 15 the box returns only in the lessons, to explain composition and the inverse. The properties that research identifies as difficult (the uniqueness of the output, the constant function, the function without a formula, two rules for one function, preimages) are posed on the machine from Grade 4; the word relation is kept for the link between two quantities, where covariation is taught; the set of ordered pairs comes back as the graph. The choices are related to the function machine as a cognitive root and to its authors' own warnings, to process-object accounts, to studies of concept images and of covariation, and to the French and IB curricula. A block-level audit of the dated source documents found the machine in only 2 of the 177 exercise blocks of Grades 7 to 10, no exercise asking pupils to draw a machine, and public chapters that opened on the relation; the revisions made after the audit are recorded with their counts before and after. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses for one are stated.

papers.title: Could This BE Any More Wrong? Teaching VLMs to Know What They Don't Know in Document Extraction
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models can extract structured fields from scanned financial documents, yet they provide no indication of when a field might be wrong. We derive per-field confidence estimates from the token log-probabilities the model already produces, via a token-to-span alignment procedure that maps logprobs onto each extracted value within the structured JSON output. Evaluated on two benchmarks (CORD v2 receipts, Kleister NDA legal contracts) with three VLM families, the minimum token probability per field achieves Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC) 0.74-0.91 for error detection, far exceeding verbalized confidence (0.53-0.56). The uncertain fields form a natural training curriculum: fine-tuning via Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves accuracy from 78.5% to 87.5% on CORD (67 examples) and from 70.7% to 75.1% on multi-page NDA contracts (259 examples), while substantially improving error detection on Kleister NDA (AUROC 0.70 to 0.85, Area Under the Accuracy-Rejection Curve (AUARC) 0.78 to 0.92). The loop requires no annotation beyond the training-split ground truth, demonstrating that confidence-guided curriculum selection transfers to complex multi-page documents when combined with native multi-image training. A frontier model (Claude Sonnet 4) used as a pseudo-label judge achieves ~92% reward agreement with ground truth on both benchmarks, suggesting this loop can operate without human annotation.

papers.title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.

papers.title: Managing Uncertainty in Teacher Vibe Coding: A Comparison of Teacher and Expert Workflows
papers.abstract: Vibe coding, or natural language software development, enables teachers to become creators of digital teaching artifacts. However, novice educators oftentimes face different barriers. This qualitative study examined the workflows of pre-service teachers, in-service teachers, and expert developers through think-aloud protocols. Findings reveal vibe coding operates through a loop of problem framing, development, and verification governed by uncertainty management. Teachers reduced uncertainty by grounding designs in authentic needs: pre-service teachers drew on pedagogical principles, whereas in-service teachers relied on everyday teaching challenges. Conversely, Experts reduced ambiguity by constraining requirements, decomposing artifacts into testable modules, and automating tests. These differences reveal complementary forms of pedagogical, contextual, and technical expertise. Future work may be about supporting nontechnical teachers in developing reliable and educational applications.

papers.title: AI-generated support, worked examples, and script-based learning in undergraduate physics: A comparative study
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support students during learning and problem solving, but its instructional value depends on how it is embedded in established learning approaches. Worked examples guide learners through the steps and reasoning of a solution; conversational AI may extend them by responding to individual questions. To isolate this added value, we compared a chatbot-delivered intelligent worked example with a matched static worked example and a lecture script. Nine recitation groups in an undergraduate electrodynamics course were cluster-randomized to the three conditions, and 86 students worked individually on a Gauss's law problem. Concept-test accuracy and self-efficacy increased significantly in all conditions, but changes did not differ significantly between groups (p=.07 for concept-test accuracy and p=.38 for self-efficacy). Four weeks later, in a reduced sample with selective participation and pre-existing group differences, students in the static worked-example condition scored higher than those in the script condition (p=.004, d=1.22), whereas the two worked-example conditions did not differ significantly. Usability, but not perceived educational value, was higher for the intelligent worked example than for the script (p=.011, d=0.88). In a subsequent homework assignment on Ampere's law with free choice of learning material (N=46), 62-71% of students in each condition reported using only the static worked example, at most 8% used exclusively the intelligent one, and 15-31% used neither. Thus, conversational delivery showed no clear additional learning benefit under the present conditions. More broadly, a learning format that is rated favorably need not be the one students voluntarily adopt.
